Who Should Write Your Small Business Website Content?

Follow a fictional Varanasi clinic as it replaces unclear content ownership with a practical responsibility map and approval workflow.

By SiteSutra · 10 November 2026

← All articlesYour next step ↓

Who should write a small business website's content? The business should own the facts, service boundaries, proof and final approval. A named writer can interview the business and turn that material into clear page copy. The designer or developer should shape the content into headings, controls, forms and responsive layouts without inventing missing claims. Put those responsibilities in writing before the build begins.

One person can hold more than one role, but the roles still need names. “The agency will handle the content” is incomplete unless the scope explains who supplies evidence, who drafts, how revisions work and who signs off on accuracy.

Meera has a homepage design but no agreed words

Imagine Meera runs a fictional physiotherapy clinic in Varanasi. The clinic, people and project are original planning examples, not a SiteSutra client story or reported result. She has approved a homepage layout and expects the website team to “add good content.” The developer expects Meera to send final copy.

A week later, the hero still contains a broad placeholder. The service cards use names copied from an old brochure. The enquiry form asks every visitor for the same information, although the reception team needs different details for appointment requests and general questions. Nobody is willing to approve a sentence about treatment because its source is unclear.

The delay is not a writing problem yet. It is an ownership problem. Meera separates the work into four stages: business facts, useful draft, page build and approval.

Assign the content roles before choosing the writer

Meera's hypothetical content responsibility map
RoleProvidesMust not assumeAcceptance evidence
Business fact ownerServices, audience, process, boundaries, service area, approved proof and response processThat a writer can discover private business facts from public pagesCurrent source notes and named approver
Writer or content leadPage purpose, hierarchy, draft copy, labels, calls to action and revision recordThat every supplied statement is current, permissioned or suitable for publicationDraft linked to sources and open questions
Designer or developerContent placement, readable structure, responsive behaviour and interface statesThat shorter placeholder text can replace an approved explanation without reviewBuilt page checked against the approved draft
Business approverAccuracy, permission, operational fit and final release decisionThat visual polish proves the words are correctDated approval with unresolved items recorded

For a small project, Meera may be the fact owner and approver while one website partner handles writing, design and development. The workflow still shows when the partner needs input and when Meera must decide.

The business supplies evidence, not polished paragraphs

Meera does not need to become a copywriter. She prepares raw material that another person can shape: the current service list, who each service suits, what happens after an enquiry, real questions the reception team hears, permitted photos, accurate credentials and statements that require professional review.

A useful fact pack can contain notes, voice transcripts, existing documents and short interviews. Each item needs a source and an owner. If a claim cannot be verified or approved, it stays out of the public draft.

This protects the website from generic language. A writer can make a sentence clearer, but only the business can confirm whether the service is actually offered, where it is available and what the team can deliver.

The writer turns evidence into a visitor decision

The writer starts with the page's job, not a word count. A service page may need to help a visitor recognise the service, understand who it is for, see what the process involves and choose the correct next step. The writer groups the facts around that decision and marks every unanswered question.

Google's guidance on people first content asks whether a site has an intended audience, a clear purpose and content that leaves a reader with enough information to move towards a goal. It also encourages clear authorship where readers would expect it. This does not mean adding keywords until the page sounds unnatural. It means giving the right visitor a complete and trustworthy explanation.

The writer should also identify the creator or accountable organisation accurately. A byline or business attribution is useful only when it reflects who is genuinely responsible for the material.

The website team edits for the interface

Approved copy rarely drops into a design without adjustment. The website team checks heading length, card capacity, button labels, mobile reading order, form instructions, empty states, errors and confirmation messages. Changes that affect meaning return to the writer and business approver.

The W3C recommends short headings that describe their sections, clear instructions and understandable error messages. Meera therefore reviews the implemented page as a visitor task, not only as a document. She checks whether someone can scan the headings, understand the service and complete the next action without guessing.

A rigid design should not force useful information into tiny boxes. If essential copy does not fit, the team revisits the component or the content structure rather than removing the fact quietly.

Choose a production model that matches your capacity

There is no universal rule that the owner, writer or website company must draft every word. Choose from three practical models:

Owner draft with professional editing

The business writes a first draft from a page brief. A writer or website partner improves structure, clarity and interface labels. This works when the owner knows the subject, can make time and is comfortable producing a complete draft.

Interview led writing

A writer interviews the fact owners, reviews supplied evidence and prepares the draft. The business answers open questions and approves accuracy. This works when expertise is available but writing time is limited.

Collaborative page workshop

The business, writer and website lead agree the visitor decision and outline together. The writer drafts, the website team prototypes and the business reviews the working page. This works when content and interaction depend closely on each other.

Whichever model Meera chooses, the commercial scope should say how many pages are included, who conducts interviews, what source material is required, how many revision rounds are included, who reviews specialist claims and what happens when input arrives late.

Use a four pass content workflow

  1. Evidence pass: collect facts, sources, permissions, customer questions and service boundaries.
  2. Structure pass: define the visitor, page purpose, sections and next action before drafting paragraphs.
  3. Draft pass: write the complete page, label open questions and record approvals.
  4. Interface pass: build the page, review it on a small screen, test every action and confirm that edits preserved meaning.

Do not wait until the final design review to discover that the business has not approved the service description. Content decisions should become more specific at each pass.

Run the five question handoff test

Before a page enters design or development, answer these questions:

  • Who is the intended visitor and what decision should the page support?
  • Which business owner confirms every service, claim and boundary?
  • Which evidence or permission supports the proof and imagery?
  • Who drafts the page and who may change its meaning during implementation?
  • Who gives final approval, and what unresolved item would stop release?

If any answer is “everyone” or “the agency,” assign a person or role before the next pass. Shared production is useful; shared accountability without ownership is not.

Create one responsibility record for the project

Download the website content responsibility matrix (CSV). Replace the sample rows with the real pages, fact owners, draft owners, evidence, approvers and review dates.

Keep approval beside the content it covers. Avoid sending sensitive customer information, passwords or unapproved personal details in a copy document. Where the subject is regulated or high risk, name the qualified reviewer and record the approved source.

Make content ownership part of the website brief

Meera does not ask the developer to invent the clinic's message, and she does not try to write every finished paragraph alone. She supplies the business truth, chooses an interview led writing model, names the professional reviewer for relevant claims and approves the working page after the reception journey is tested.
